title: The Binding of Isaac: God Will Provide
summary: God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer Isaac, his only son whom he loves, as a burnt offering on a mountain in the land of Moriah. Abraham obeys, binds Isaac on the altar, and raises the knife, but the angel of the LORD stops him, and Abraham sacrifices a ram caught in a thicket in his son's place. God swears by himself to bless Abraham and bless all nations through his offspring, and the chapter closes with news of Nahor's family, including Rebekah.
story: Everything in Abraham's story has pointed toward Isaac. The promises of a nation, of descendants like the stars, and of blessing for all peoples all run through this one boy. Now God asks for him. The chapter is the climax of Abraham's life of faith, and it began with a command to “go” to a land God would show him (Genesis 12:1); it ends with the same kind of command and a mountain God will show him. After this, the story begins to turn toward the next generation. The list of Nahor's children at the end quietly introduces Rebekah, who will become Isaac's wife in Genesis 24.
historical:
The land of Moriah is not otherwise identified in Genesis. Second Chronicles 3:1 says that Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem “on Mount Moriah,” and Jewish and Christian tradition has long identified Abraham's mountain with the temple mount. The Samaritans, by contrast, associated the event with Mount Gerizim. A trip of three days from Beersheba to the Jerusalem area, roughly eighty kilometers (about fifty miles), fits the text.

Child sacrifice was a real practice in parts of the ancient world. Second Kings 3:27 records the king of Moab offering his firstborn son on the city wall in a crisis, and infant burials at Phoenician Carthage have long been debated as evidence of sacrifice. Israel's law forbade the practice absolutely (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31), and the prophets condemned it as something God never commanded or even imagined (Jeremiah 7:31). Genesis doesn't give Isaac's age. He is old enough to carry the wood, and later Jewish tradition gave him various ages; Josephus, the first-century Jewish historian, made him twenty-five.
cultural:
A burnt offering was a sacrifice wholly consumed by fire on the altar, given entirely to God. Abraham carries what the ritual requires: fire, a knife, wood, and he builds an altar on the spot. The ram caught by its horns, offered “in place of his son” (verse 13), introduces the idea of a substitute that will run through Israel's sacrificial system. In Jewish tradition the chapter is called the Akedah, the binding, from the verb in verse 9. It is read in synagogues at Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, when the ram's horn (the shofar) is sounded, and it has shaped Jewish reflection on faithfulness and martyrdom for centuries.

Firstborn sons held a special place in the ancient Near East as heirs and bearers of the family's future. Later Israelite law claimed every firstborn as belonging to God, but required that firstborn sons be redeemed rather than sacrificed (Exodus 13:13).
literary: This is one of the most tightly written narratives in the Bible. The narrator tells us at once that it is a test, but Abraham doesn't know that, and the text refuses to show his feelings. The command piles up its weight in stages: “your son,” “your only son Isaac,” “whom you love.” The Hebrew phrase for go in verse 2 is the same unusual phrase used in Genesis 12:1, and “which I will show you” repeats that call too. Abraham's answer, “Here I am,” comes three times, to God (verse 1), to Isaac (verse 7), and to the angel (verse 11). The line “the two of them walked on together” frames Isaac's question and Abraham's answer. The chapter turns on the verb to see: God will see to (provide) the lamb (verse 8), Abraham looks up and sees the ram (verse 13), and he names the place The LORD Will Provide. The closing genealogy gives Nahor twelve sons, like Ishmael and later Jacob.

outline.t: Three days to the mountain; “God Himself will provide”
Isaac bound, the angel intervenes, a ram in his place
God swears by himself to bless Abraham
News of Nahor's family and the birth of Rebekah

doctrines.note: Abraham's faith is tested at the point where God's command seems to contradict God's promise. He tells his servants, “we will return to you” (verse 5), and Hebrews 11:19 says he reasoned that God could raise the dead. Faith here trusts the Promiser more than the promised gift.

The ram dies “in place of his son” (verse 13). The chapter introduces the principle of substitution that the sacrificial system will develop and the New Testament will apply to Christ's death. God himself provides the offering.

God confirms his promises with an oath: “By Myself I have sworn” (verse 16), since there is no one greater to swear by (Hebrews 6:13). The promise that all nations will be blessed through Abraham's offspring is restated here as the covenant's goal.

words.note: Nasah, to test or prove. It describes putting someone to the proof to reveal what is really there, as God later tests Israel in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 8:2). The test isn't God finding out something he didn't know, but bringing Abraham's trust into the open, as the angel's “now I know that you fear God” expresses in human terms.

Yachid, only, one and only. Isaac was not Abraham's only child, since Ishmael lived, but he was the only son of the promise, the unique and irreplaceable heir. The word is repeated in verses 2, 12, and 16. The Greek translation rendered it beloved, while Hebrews 11:17 calls Isaac Abraham's one and only son with the same Greek word John uses of Jesus in John 3:16.

The name Abraham gives the place, YHWH Yireh, The LORD Will Provide, uses the ordinary verb to see. To see to something is to provide it. Abraham had said God would see to the lamb (verse 8), and God did. The saying that followed, “On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided,” became a proverb of hope.

christ: Christians have read this chapter in the light of the cross from the beginning. Paul's words in Romans 8:32, “He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,” echo the Greek translation of Genesis 22:12 and 16, where Abraham did not withhold his son. The Greek translation of verse 2 calls Isaac Abraham's beloved son, and many hear that phrase behind the voice from heaven at Jesus' baptism calling him the beloved Son. Hebrews 11:17-19 says Abraham, in a sense, received Isaac back from death. Early Christian interpreters noticed further patterns: a beloved son carrying the wood up a hill, a place of sacrifice associated with Jerusalem, and a lamb provided by God, which John the Baptist names when he calls Jesus “the Lamb of God.” The great difference is also the point. Isaac was spared at the last moment, and a substitute died in his place; God did not spare his own Son. Finally, the promise of verse 18 is read by Paul as the gospel announced in advance (Galatians 3:8, 16).

hard.q: How could God command a father to sacrifice his son?
hard.a:
This is one of the hardest chapters in the Bible, and honest readers of every tradition have felt its weight. The Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard built a whole book, Fear and Trembling (1843), around the terror of Abraham's obedience, arguing that it cannot be made comfortable. Several things in the text shape how Christians and Jews have read it.

First, the narrator tells the reader at the outset that this is a test (verse 1), and God stops it before any harm is done. The story does not portray a God who wants children killed; its outcome is that he doesn't. In a world where some peoples offered children to their gods, the chapter shows the true God refusing the sacrifice and providing a substitute, and Israel's later law and prophets condemn child sacrifice outright. Second, the test concerns whether Abraham trusts God's promise, which ran through Isaac, more than he clings to the gift itself. His words to the servants, “we will return to you” (verse 5), and the reading in Hebrews 11:19 suggest he expected God to keep his word even through death. Third, Christians see the story's full meaning in what God himself did: he asked of Abraham what he did not in the end require, and gave what Abraham was spared from giving. None of this removes the difficulty entirely, and the text doesn't ask us to.

questions: Abraham was asked to trust God with the very thing God had promised him. What gift in your life is hardest to hold with an open hand?
Isaac asked, “where is the lamb for the burnt offering?” How does the answer of this chapter shape the way you think about God's provision?
The chapter leaves Abraham's feelings unspoken. Why might the narrator have chosen silence, and how does that affect the way you read it?
